# equation.io

> Free in-browser graphing calculator (WebGL). Plots 2D curves, inequality
> regions, scalar fields, vector fields and ODEs, complex functions (including
> domain coloring, conformal maps and escape-time fractals), 3D surfaces,
> parametric curves/surfaces, plane geometry (named draggable points,
> segments, polylines, vector arrows, polygons, squares, circles), symbolic
> derivatives and integrals,
> and random variables with shaded probabilities. No account, no server round-trips: the graph state
> lives in the URL fragment, so you can construct a link that opens the app
> with any set of equations already rendered.

## Deep links

Format:

    https://equation.io/g/<equation>;<equation>;...

- Percent-encode each equation (JavaScript `encodeURIComponent`), then
  additionally escape ( ) ! ' * as %28 %29 %21 %27 %2A — chat apps cut
  auto-linked URLs at bare parentheses, silently truncating the graph.
- Encoded equations are joined with `;`, and that literal `;` is only ever the
  row separator (a reader also accepts `%3B` there, since clients re-encode
  it). A `;` that belongs to an equation — inside quoted text, like
  `p[p.city == "a;b"]` or `open("sales;2026.csv")` — is encoded TWICE, as
  `%253B`, so the two can never be confused: the payload encodes the quotes
  too, and a singly-encoded one comes back as a row separator, splitting the
  equation in half.
- Every equation gets its own row and color. Definitions (constants,
  functions, coordinate fields) are rows too — order does not matter.
- `/g/` links unfurl with a rendered preview image (og:image) in chat apps
  and social cards; the image itself is served at
  `https://equation.io/api/og/<same payload>`. An equivalent fragment form,
  `https://equation.io/#<same payload>`, also opens the graph and keeps the
  equations out of server logs, but gets no preview card.

Examples (paste-ready):

- [Parabola](https://equation.io/#y%3Dx%5E2): `y = x^2`
- [Circle](https://equation.io/#x%5E2%2By%5E2%3D4): `x^2 + y^2 = 4`
- [Cubic + tangent line](https://equation.io/#f(x)%3Dx%5E3-2x;g(x)%3Dd%2Fdx%20f(x);a%3D1;y%3Df(x);y%3Df(a)%2Bg(a)(x-a)): `f(x) = x^3 - 2x; g(x) = d/dx f(x); a = 1; y = f(x); y = f(a) + g(a)(x-a)`
- [Slider-controlled wave](https://equation.io/#a%3D2;y%3Dsin(a%20x)%2Fa): `a = 2; y = sin(a x)/a`
- [Fourier series](https://equation.io/#N%20%3D%208;y%20%3D%202%20sum%5Bn%3D1..N%5D%20(-1)%5E(n%2B1)%20sin(n%20x)%2Fn): `N = 8; y = 2 sum[n=1..N] (-1)^(n+1) sin(n x)/n` — drag N for more harmonics
- [Animated ripples](https://equation.io/#sin(x%5E2%2By%5E2-4t)%2F2): `sin(x^2+y^2-4t)/2`
- [3D saddle](https://equation.io/#z%20%3D%20x%5E2%20-%20y%5E2): `z = x^2 - y^2`
- [Torus (parametric 3D)](https://equation.io/#(cos(2pi%20u)(2%2Bcos(2pi%20v))%2C%20sin(2pi%20u)(2%2Bcos(2pi%20v))%2C%20sin(2pi%20v))): `(cos(2pi u)(2+cos(2pi v)), sin(2pi u)(2+cos(2pi v)), sin(2pi v))`
- [Complex dipole field](https://equation.io/#ln(w-2)-ln(w%2B2)): `ln(w-2) - ln(w+2)`
- [Domain coloring](https://equation.io/#domain((w%5E3%20-%201)%2Fw)): `domain((w^3 - 1)/w)`
- [Conformal grid image](https://equation.io/#conformal(w%5E2%2F4)): `conformal(w^2/4)`
- [Mandelbrot set](https://equation.io/#iter(z%5E2%20%2B%20w)): `iter(z^2 + w)`
- [Julia set](https://equation.io/#iter(z%5E2%20-%200.7269%20%2B%200.1889i)): `iter(z^2 - 0.7269 + 0.1889i)`
- [Koch snowflake (recursive function)](https://equation.io/#f(z)%20%3D%20%7Bre(z)%20%3E%3D%201%3A%201%2C%20f(4%20-%203(z%5E6)%5E(1%2F6))%7D;f(x%20i%20-%20%7Cy%7C)%20%3E%3D%200): `f(z) = {re(z) >= 1: 1, f(4 - 3(z^6)^(1/6))}; f(x i - |y|) >= 0` — a tail-recursive function shades where its recursion terminates
- [Vector field](https://equation.io/#(-y%2C%20x)): `(-y, x)` — drawn as animated streamlines
- [Pendulum phase portrait](https://equation.io/#(x'%2C%20y')%20%3D%20(y%2C%20-sin(x))): `(x', y') = (y, -sin(x))`
- [Slope field](https://equation.io/#y'%20%3D%20x%20-%20y): `y' = x - y`
- [Polar cardioid](https://equation.io/#r%3Dsqrt(x%5E2%2By%5E2);theta%3Datan2(y%2Cx);r%3D2(1%2Bcos(theta))): `r = sqrt(x^2+y^2); theta = atan2(y,x); r = 2(1 + cos(theta))`
- [Circle through a draggable point](https://equation.io/#C%20%3D%20(0%2C%200);P%20%3D%20(2%2C%201);circle(C%2C%20%7CP%20-%20C%7C);segment(C%2C%20P)): `C = (0, 0); P = (2, 1); circle(C, |P - C|); segment(C, P)`
- [Triangle: a side and its angles](https://equation.io/#A%20%3D%20(-2%2C%20-1);B%20%3D%20(3%2C%20-0.5);C%20%3D%20(0.5%2C%202.5);polygon(A%2C%20B%2C%20C);distance(A%2C%20B);angle(B%2C%20A%2C%20C)%20180%2Fpi;angle(B%2C%20A%2C%20C)%20%2B%20angle(C%2C%20B%2C%20A)%20%2B%20angle(A%2C%20C%2C%20B)): `A = (-2, -1); B = (3, -0.5); C = (0.5, 2.5); polygon(A, B, C); distance(A, B); angle(B, A, C) 180/pi; angle(B, A, C) + angle(C, B, A) + angle(A, C, B)` — distance() and angle() are numbers, so the bare rows read out "= value" and follow the points as you drag; the angle sum stays π (−π once the triangle turns clockwise: angles are signed)
- [Vector sum (parallelogram rule)](https://equation.io/#A%20%3D%20(3%2C%201);B%20%3D%20(1%2C%202);vector(A);vector(B);vector(A%20%2B%20B);polyline(A%2C%20A%20%2B%20B%2C%20B)): `A = (3, 1); B = (1, 2); vector(A); vector(B); vector(A + B); polyline(A, A + B, B)` — vector() draws arrows (from the origin with one argument), polyline() the open path completing the parallelogram; drag A or B
- [Thébault's theorem (squares on a parallelogram)](https://equation.io/#A%20%3D%20(0%2C%200);B%20%3D%20(4%2C%200.5);D%20%3D%20(1%2C%202.5);C%20%3D%20B%20%2B%20D%20-%20A;polygon(A%2C%20B%2C%20C%2C%20D);square(B%2C%20A);square(C%2C%20B);square(D%2C%20C);square(A%2C%20D);P%20%3D%20midpoint(A%2C%20B)%20-%20perp(B%20-%20A)%2F2;Q%20%3D%20midpoint(B%2C%20C)%20-%20perp(C%20-%20B)%2F2;R%20%3D%20midpoint(C%2C%20D)%20-%20perp(D%20-%20C)%2F2;S%20%3D%20midpoint(D%2C%20A)%20-%20perp(A%20-%20D)%2F2;polygon(P%2C%20Q%2C%20R%2C%20S)): `A = (0, 0); B = (4, 0.5); D = (1, 2.5); C = B + D - A; polygon(A, B, C, D); square(B, A); square(C, B); square(D, C); square(A, D); P = midpoint(A, B) - perp(B - A)/2; …; polygon(P, Q, R, S)` — drag A, B or D; the square centers stay a square
- [Normal probability](https://equation.io/#m%20%3D%201;s%20%3D%200.5;X%20~%20Normal(m%2C%20s);P(0%20%3C%20X%20%3C%202)): `m = 1; s = 0.5; X ~ Normal(m, s); P(0 < X < 2)` — the density with the area between 0 and 2 shaded; drag m or s and the probability follows
- [Swinging pendulum (integrated state)](https://equation.io/#th'%20%3D%20om;om'%20%3D%20-sin(th)%20-%20om%2F8;th(0)%20%3D%203;bob%20%3D%20(sin(th)%2C%20-cos(th));segment((0%2C%200)%2C%20bob);bob): `th' = om; om' = -sin(th) - om/8; th(0) = 3; bob = (sin(th), -cos(th)); segment((0, 0), bob); bob` — th is the angle, om the angular velocity; segment() draws the rod, the named point draws the bob
- [Double pendulum](https://equation.io/#g%20%3D%209.8;L1%20%3D%201;L2%20%3D%201;m1%20%3D%201;m2%20%3D%201;M%20%3D%20(((m1%2Bm2)%20L1%2C%20m2%20L2%20cos(th_1%20-%20th_2))%2C%20(L1%20cos(th_1%20-%20th_2)%2C%20L2));f%20%3D%20(-m2%20L2%20om_2%5E2%20sin(th_1%20-%20th_2)%20-%20(m1%2Bm2)%20g%20sin(th_1)%2C%20L1%20om_1%5E2%20sin(th_1%20-%20th_2)%20-%20g%20sin(th_2));th'%20%3D%20om;om'%20%3D%20solve(M%2C%20f);th(0)%20%3D%20(2.5%2C%202.4);b1%20%3D%20(L1%20sin(th_1)%2C%20-L1%20cos(th_1));b2%20%3D%20b1%20%2B%20(L2%20sin(th_2)%2C%20-L2%20cos(th_2));segment((0%2C%200)%2C%20b1);segment(b1%2C%20b2);b1;b2): `M = (((m1+m2) L1, m2 L2 cos(th_1 - th_2)), (L1 cos(th_1 - th_2), L2)); f = (…); th' = om; om' = solve(M, f); th(0) = (2.5, 2.4); …` — the Lagrangian form M(θ)ω′ = f: th and om are 2-vector states with components th_1, th_2; solve() is Cramer's rule; segment()s between named bob points draw the linkage
- [Orbit (vector gravity)](https://equation.io/#r'%20%3D%20vel;vel'%20%3D%20-9%20r%2F%7Cr%7C%5E3;r(0)%20%3D%20(2%2C%200);vel(0)%20%3D%20(0%2C%201.5);segment((0%2C%200)%2C%20r);r;(0%2C%200)): `r' = vel; vel' = -9 r/|r|^3; r(0) = (2, 0); vel(0) = (0, 1.5); segment((0, 0), r); r; (0, 0)` — vector states with point arithmetic; the bare state name draws as a moving point
- [Rössler attractor (state family + orbit)](https://equation.io/#a%20%3D%200.2;b%20%3D%200.2;c%20%3D%205.7;k%20%3D%204;p'%20%3D%20k%20(-p_2%20-%20p_3%2C%20p_1%20%2B%20a%20p_2%2C%20b%20%2B%20p_3%20(p_1%20-%20c));s%20%3D%202pi%20sort(%5B0..299%5D)%2F300;p(0)%20%3D%20(8cos(s)%2C%208sin(s)%2C%200);p%5B1%5D(10..100);p;camera(-0.9%2C%200.35%2C%2045%2C%20(0%2C%200%2C%207))): `p' = k (-p_2 - p_3, p_1 + a p_2, b + p_3 (p_1 - c)); s = 2pi sort([0..299])/300; p(0) = (8cos(s), 8sin(s), 0); p[1](10..100); p` — a tuple of starting values runs 300 copies of the system, in order; `p[1](10..100)` draws one run's path over that time as the attractor, and `p` the 300 particles flowing along it; k speeds the flow up
- [Matrix phase portrait](https://equation.io/#a%20%3D%20-1;b%20%3D%20-1%2F4;A%20%3D%20((0%2C%201)%2C%20(a%2C%20b));(x'%2C%20y')%20%3D%20A%20(x%2C%20y)): `a = -1; b = -1/4; A = ((0, 1), (a, b)); (x', y') = A (x, y)` — a linear system as its literal matrix, sliders in the entries
- [Poisson: strict versus non-strict](https://equation.io/#m%20%3D%204;X%20~%20Poisson(m);P(X%20%3C%203);P(X%20%3C%3D%203);P(X%20%3D%203)): `m = 4; X ~ Poisson(m); P(X < 3); P(X <= 3); P(X = 3)` — a discrete variable draws its pmf as stems; each P(…) row highlights exactly the stems it counts, so `<` stops at 2, `<=` takes the stem at 3, and `P(X = 3)` is that one stem
- [Two dice](https://equation.io/#X%20~%20DiscreteUniform(1%2C%206);Y%20~%20DiscreteUniform(1%2C%206);S%20%3D%20X%20%2B%20Y;P(S%20%3E%3D%2010);P(X%20%3E%20Y);P(X%20%3E%3D%20Y);E(S)): `X ~ DiscreteUniform(1, 6); Y ~ DiscreteUniform(1, 6); S = X + Y; P(S >= 10); P(X > Y); P(X >= Y); E(S)` — arithmetic over discrete variables is exact: the sum's pmf is the triangle on 2…12, drawn as stems; `P(X > Y)` = 15/36 and `P(X >= Y)` = 21/36 differ by the ties, `P(X = Y)`
- [Central limit theorem](https://equation.io/#X1%20~%20Uniform%280%2C%201%29;X2%20~%20Uniform%280%2C%201%29;X3%20~%20Uniform%280%2C%201%29;X4%20~%20Uniform%280%2C%201%29;S%20%3D%20X1%20%2B%20X2%20%2B%20X3%20%2B%20X4;Z%20~%20Normal%282%2C%20sqrt%281%2F3%29%29;P%28S%20%3E%203%29): `X1 ~ Uniform(0, 1); X2 ~ Uniform(0, 1); X3 ~ Uniform(0, 1); X4 ~ Uniform(0, 1); S = X1 + X2 + X3 + X4; Z ~ Normal(2, sqrt(1/3)); P(S > 3)` — the sum of four uniforms hugs the matching normal
- [Conditional random variable](https://equation.io/#X%20~%20Normal%280%2C%201%29;Y%20%3D%20%7BX%20%3E%200%3A%20X%5E2%2C%201%7D;P%28Y%20%3E%200.5%29;P%28Y%20%3E%20X%29): `X ~ Normal(0, 1); Y = {X > 0: X^2, 1}; P(Y > 0.5); P(Y > X)` — a piecewise transform of X, with probabilities of derived and joint events

## Share links with preview images (/g/)

The same payload also works as a path, and this form unfurls with a rendered
preview image (og:image) in chat apps and social cards:

    https://equation.io/g/<equation>;<equation>;...

Prefer the `/g/` form when the link will be posted somewhere that shows link
previews; prefer the `#` form otherwise (it keeps the equations out of server
logs). Both open the same app with the same graph. The preview image itself is
served at `https://equation.io/api/og/<same payload>`.

## MCP server

An MCP endpoint (Streamable HTTP) lives at:

    https://equation.io/mcp

Tools: `encode_graph_url` (validates each equation through the app's own parser,
returns url/share_url plus per-row classification or errors, with text-only MCP responses. Share links still provide a PNG preview; rows the preview renderer cannot draw are
listed in `preview_omits` with the reason — the live app renders more than
the static preview, so an omission never means the row failed) and
`decode_graph_url` (decodes an existing link back into its equation rows so you can
edit a user's graph and build a new link). This document is also served as
the server's `syntax` MCP resource, so the full reference can be pulled on
demand instead of living in a tool description. No authentication required.

Use `show_graph` to display the interactive graph directly in an MCP Apps host
such as ChatGPT web. It accepts the same `equations` array and returns per-row
validation and share links plus an associated UI resource. It does not include
`preview` / `preview_omits` — those describe the share-link card on
`encode_graph_url`, not the widget.
The widget supports editing, sliders, zoom, and 3D rotation; edits update the
model's context with the complete current equations and share_url. Preserve
those edited rows on follow-up requests. Use `encode_graph_url` for validation
or link-only requests. Clients without MCP Apps support can open share_url.

## Expression syntax

- Operators: `+ - * / ^`, parentheses, unary minus. Multiplication is
  implicit: `2x`, `x y`, `2cos(t)`, `a(x-1)` all work. After a `/`, spacing
  groups: factors written touching stay in the divisor (`1/2pi` is 1/(2π),
  `x^2/2s^2` is x²/(2s²), `1/x(x+1)` is 1/(x(x+1))), while a space ends it
  (`g/L sin(th)` is (g/L)·sin(th), `1/2 m v^2` is m v²/2, `(y - b)/h (x - a)`
  is a slope times (x - a)). `·` and `×` multiply
  numbers too, and between two vectors are the dot and cross product (see
  Vector calculus); `⊗` and `∧` are the outer and wedge products (see
  Tensors). All four bind like `*`.
- Absolute value bars: `|x|`, including nested/multiplied forms like `2|x-1|`.
- Unicode: Greek letters are ordinary names (`θ = 1` makes a θ slider; `Δx`
  is a name like `dx`), superscript digits are exponents (`x³` is `x^3`,
  `x⁻²` is `x^(-2)`), and subscript digits are the `_` subscript syntax in
  its unicode spelling — `T₀` IS `T_0`, so `r₁` reads a vector state's `r_1`
  component and `a₃` a sequence's third term. A single name or number in
  braces is the same subscript: `T_{c}` is `T_c`, `a_{10}` is `a_10`.
  `·`, `⋅`, `×`, `÷`, `−`, `≤`,
  `≥`, `≠` mean their ASCII counterparts (`⊗` is `outer(a, b)`, `∧` is
  `wedge(a, b)`; the editor types them from `\otimes` and `\wedge`). π never joins a longer name,
  so `2πr` is 2·π·r. In the editor, typing `\pi`, `\theta`, `\nabla`, …
  inserts the symbol itself, and a `\` before any built-in function name
  simply drops (`\sin(x)` → `sin(x)`, `\trail` → `trail`), so `\` also works
  as a function search.
- Constants: `pi`, `e` (π also parses directly; τ and `tau` are ordinary
  names, free to define), and the unit
  vectors `e_x`, `e_y`, `e_z` = `(1,0,0)`, `(0,1,0)`, `(0,0,1)` (always 3D,
  so a row using one is a 3D scene; defining `e_x` yourself replaces it).
  Imaginary unit `i` in complex expressions.
- Functions: sin cos tan asin acos atan atan2(y,x) sinh cosh tanh sech coth
  asinh acosh atanh sqrt abs exp ln (natural) log (base 10) log2 floor ceil round
  min max mod sign fract sinc gamma factorial, complex helpers re im arg conj,
  and point helpers dot cross perp midpoint unit. Also `erf(x)`,
  `normalpdf(x, mean, sd)` and `normalcdf(x, mean, sd)`; `gcd(a, b)`, the
  greatest common divisor of whole numbers (other arguments round to the
  nearest one), so `1/gcd(floor(x), floor(y))` is 1 on the coprime cells of
  the grid; and `isprime(n)`, 1 for a prime and 0 otherwise
  (`a_n = isprime(n)`), which gives no value past 2048² − 1 rather than
  guess. Vector calculus has `grad`, `div`, `curl`, `laplacian`, `jacobian`
  and `hessian`, and the geometry of a curve `curvature`, `torsion`,
  `osculating` and `frame` (all below).
  Function names are
  case-insensitive: `Sin(x)`, `SQRT(x)` and `sin(x)` are the same call. Always
  use parentheses for arguments — write `sin(x)`, not `sin x`.
- Factorial: postfix `!` — `5!` is 120, `y = x!` plots Γ(x+1), `2^3!` is 2^6.
  Non-integers use the Gamma function; negative integers are undefined.
- Piecewise: `{x < 0: -x, x >= 0: x^2}` — `cond: value` cases tried in order,
  with an optional last bare value as the default (`{0 < x < 1: 1, 0}`).
  Conditions are inequalities and may chain. With no default the value is
  undefined wherever no case holds and nothing is drawn there, which makes
  one case a domain restriction: `y = {0 < x < 2: x^2}` plots the parabola
  on (0, 2) only. It works in any row kind — `x^2 + y^2 = {x > 0: 16}` is a
  half circle, `(2cos(u), {sin(u) > 0: 2sin(u)})` cuts a parametric curve.
  A bare condition is a case worth 1, as in Desmos: `{x > 0, 5}` is
  `{x > 0: 1, 5}`. Values may be complex (`{x > 0: w, conj(w)}`); the
  conditions themselves compare real values (`re(w) > 0`, `|w| < 1`).
  A condition can be named and reused: `r = x^2 + y^2 + z^2`;
  `within = r < 16`; `x + y = {within: 1}` — the name reads as the
  inequality it stands for, in a function body too (its x is the plane's,
  not the function's parameter), and filters reductions: `count(within)`,
  `mean({within: x})` (in a function body, a filter whose condition reads a
  parameter's name is an error: rename the parameter). The definition draws nothing; a row of just the
  name draws what the inequality would; arithmetic on it is an error. A
  function may return a condition too: `inside(p) = p < 2`;
  `y = {inside(x): x^2}`. A name as a bare condition needs a `cond: value`
  part beside it, `{within, x > 0: 1}`: `{within, 5}` is a tuple, so write
  `{within: 1, 5}`.
- Vector calculus: these operators expand symbolically like d/dx, so
  sliders and t work inside them.
  - `grad(f)` is the tuple (∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y), plus ∂f/∂z when f uses z:
    `grad(x^2 - y^2)` plots as a vector field.
  - `div(F)` is ∂F₁/∂x + ∂F₂/∂y (+ ∂F₃/∂z), a scalar field:
    `div((x y, y^2))`.
  - `curl(F)` of a 3D field is a vector field: `curl((y z, -x z, 0))`. Of a
    plane field it is the scalar ∂F₂/∂x − ∂F₁/∂y: `curl((-y, x))` is 2.
  - `laplacian(f)` is div(grad(f)), for a scalar f: `laplacian(x^2 + y^2)`
    is 4.
  - `jacobian(F)` is the matrix of partials, row i the gradient of F's
    component i (2 components: over x, y; 3: over x, y, z), and `hessian(f)`
    the matrix of second partials of a scalar f. A 2×2 one in x and y draws
    as a matrix field: `jacobian((x^2 - y^2, 2 x y))` is all circles, the
    mark of a conformal map.
  - With ∇ (in the editor, type `\nabla`): `∇f` is grad(f), `∇·F` is div(F),
    `∇×F` is curl(F), and `∇²f` (or `∇^2 f`) is laplacian(f). ∇ takes the
    rest of the product, as d/dx does: `∇ x^2 y` and `∇f(x, y)`.
  - Names work as arguments. With `f(x, y) = x^2 - y^2`, `grad(f)` and `∇f`
    mean grad(f(x, y)). With a field `r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2)`, `grad(1/r)`
    differentiates through r (so does `d/dx r`). With a named vector
    `F = (-y, x)`, `curl(F)` and `∇×F` work.
  - The Laplacian of a vector field is not supported. grad of a vector and
    div or curl of a scalar are errors.
  - Between two vectors, `A · B` (also `⋅`) is dot(A, B) and `A × B` is
    cross(A, B). `*` between vectors is an error, since it could mean either.
    `·` binds like `*`, so `∇f · (1, 1)/sqrt(2)` is a directional
    derivative.
- Fourier analysis: `fourier(signal)` draws a one-sided amplitude spectrum
  as points (frequency, amplitude). The signal is either a real expression
  over one interval, which is its variable and its period —
  `s = interval(0, 1); fourier(sin(2pi s))`, or `fourier(f(s))` for a
  function f — or ordered, equally spaced real samples
  (`fourier((0, 1, 0, -1))`). A signal in x (`fourier(sin(2pi x))`) or a
  bare function name (`fourier(f)`) is an error that shows the interval
  form: nothing binds x for you. A bracket list is an unordered multiset;
  give samples as a tuple. For CSV row order, use
  `S = sort(data.signal, data.row); fourier(S)`; rows must be equally spaced.
  `sort(data.signal)` sorts by VALUE and changes the signal.
  - The interval interval(lo, hi) is one period [lo, hi): frequency is in
    cycles per unit of it, bins k/(hi-lo), from DC through Nyquist.
    Amplitude is the sinusoid's peak amplitude; DC is the absolute mean,
    and DC and an even-length Nyquist bin are not doubled. No window is
    applied. A nonperiodic endpoint mismatch causes spectral leakage.
  - A signal over an interval uses 256 equally spaced samples; an optional
    second argument sets a whole sample count from 2 to 4096:
    `s = interval(0, 2pi); fourier(sin(3s), 512)`. The endpoint hi is
    excluded. Samples span [0, 1), or the interval given after them:
    `fourier(S, interval(0, 10))`; they use their own length (2–4096), so
    give no sample count. Odd lengths and non-powers of two work.
  - `reconstruct(signal, N)` returns a periodic real expression in x:
    its signed mean plus frequency bins 1 through N, with phase preserved
    and the signal's interval as the period. Draw it with
    `y = reconstruct(f(s), N)`. N is a whole number from 0 to
    min(128, floor(sample count/2)); N = 0 is the mean. Use a bounded
    slider such as `N = clamp(round(5), 0, 48)` to add harmonics.
    The optional sample count, or a tuple's interval, follows N:
    `y = reconstruct(f(s), N, 512)`. Defaults match fourier.
    At full available N, the reconstruction interpolates the samples;
    discontinuities can exhibit Gibbs overshoot.
  - Coefficients are numeric approximations computed when the document
    changes. Static sliders in signals or interval bounds recompute them;
    signals cannot depend on t or simulation states. Missing/nonfinite
    samples are errors, rather than removed (removing them would change
    spacing). CSV data stays device-local in shared links, like other data
    plots.
  - Name a spectrum to draw stems with existing geometry:
    `S = fourier(f(s)); segment((S.x, 0), S); S`. Use split views with a shared
    x axis for the original and reconstruction; the spectrum has its own
    frequency axis. The Fourier analysis examples demonstrate all three.
- Curves: the differential geometry of a parametric curve in u — a tuple
  `(f(u), g(u))` or `(f(u), g(u), h(u))`, a named one `C = (…)`, or a
  function of one parameter `f(s) = (…)`. These expand symbolically like
  d/dx, so sliders and t work inside them.
  - `curvature(C, u0)` reads out κ at u = u0. In the plane it is signed,
    positive where the curve turns left (counterclockwise):
    `curvature((u, u^2), 0)` is 2, and `curvature((2cos(u), -2sin(u)), 0)`
    is −0.5. In space it is |r′ × r″|/|r′|³ ≥ 0.
  - `torsion(C, u0)` of a space curve: how fast it twists out of its
    osculating plane. The helix `C = (2cos(u), 2sin(u), u)` has curvature
    0.4 and torsion 0.2 everywhere. A plane curve has none (an error).
  - Without u0 both are functions of u, for use in other rows:
    `(u, curvature(C))` plots κ against u, and `k(u) = curvature(C, u)`
    names it. Alone on a row (or `1/curvature(C)`) they are an error that
    says so (a row in u alone would draw the density of its values). A
    list u0 reads each point: `curvature(C, [0.2, 0.4])`.
  - `osculating(C, u0)` draws the osculating circle at u = u0: through the
    point, radius 1/|κ|, centred on the concave side. A space curve's lies in
    its osculating plane. Where κ = 0 (an inflection) it is the tangent line,
    and near one a large circle that flattens into it. A list u0 draws one
    circle per point.
  - `frame(C, u0)` draws the Frenet frame at u = u0 as unit arrows from the
    point: T (tangent), N and, in space, B = T × N; one point at a time. In
    the plane N is T turned left (with κ signed, κN points toward the centre
    of curvature); in space N points toward the centre, and N and B are
    undefined where κ = 0. With t for u0 it rides along; a `C` row draws u from 0 to 1,
    so trace the curve once over that and wrap t into it:
    `C = (2cos(2pi u), sin(2pi u))`, `C`, `frame(C, t/10)`,
    `osculating(C, t/10)` (u0 past 1 is the same point again).
- Surfaces: the curvature of a parametric surface in u and v — a tuple
  `(f(u, v), g(u, v), h(u, v))`, a named one `S = (…)`, or a function of two
  parameters. Expanded symbolically from the first and second fundamental
  forms like `curvature(C)`, so sliders and t work inside them (central
  differences stand in where a part cannot be differentiated: floor, gamma).
  - `gaussian(S)` is the Gaussian curvature K = (LN − M²)/(EG − F²), a
    function of u and v; `gaussian(S, u0, v0)` (or `gaussian(S, (u0, v0))`,
    `gaussian(S, P)`) reads it at a point. The sphere of radius R has
    K = 1/R² everywhere; the saddle `(u, v, u^2 - v^2)` has −4 at (0, 0); a
    torus `((3 + cos(v)) cos(u), (3 + cos(v)) sin(u), sin(v))` has
    cos(v)/(3 + cos(v)): positive on the outside, negative round the hole.
  - `meancurvature(S)` is the mean curvature H = (EN − 2FM + GL)/(2(EG − F²)),
    with the normal ∂S/∂u × ∂S/∂v: H is negative where the surface bends away
    from that normal, so the sphere `(R cos(v) cos(u), R cos(v) sin(u),
    R sin(v))`, whose normal points out, has H = −1/R (swap u and v and it is
    +1/R). Minimal surfaces (catenoid, helicoid, Enneper's) have H = 0.
  - Alone on a row, `gaussian(S)` (or `meancurvature(S)`) draws S coloured
    by it on a diverging scale: toward the row's colour where it is
    positive, its complement where negative, grey at 0, scaled to the
    surface's typical size of it (so read values with the point form). With
    `u = interval(0, 2pi)` and `v = interval(0, 2pi)` above, the torus is
    `S = ((3 + cos(v)) cos(u), (3 + cos(v)) sin(u), sin(v))` and `gaussian(S)`.
    Elsewhere they are numbers in u and v: `(u, v, gaussian(S))` is K as a
    height over the parameter square.
  - On a panel drawn on a surface (an `on(…)` row), `gaussian(x, y)` and
    `meancurvature(x, y)` are K and H of that surface in the panel's x and
    y: a scalar field painted on it on the same diverging scale, read on
    hover; `gaussian(P)` or `gaussian(0.5, 1)` is the number at a point.
  - `geodesic(S, (u0, v0), (du, dv))` draws the geodesic of S — the
    straightest curve on it — from the point at (u0, v0) in the direction
    (du, dv), given in u and v. It is integrated in the background as it is
    drawn (the last one stays on screen until the next is ready), at unit
    speed along the surface, from the geodesic equations with the
    Christoffel symbols of S's metric (expanded symbolically). A fourth
    argument is its length on the surface (`geodesic(S, P, (1, 0), 5)`;
    negative runs backwards); without it, it runs twice the size of the
    surface's bounding box. It stops where it leaves u's and v's ranges
    (0..1, or their intervals) — except across a range the surface repeats
    over, like a torus's angles or a sphere's longitude, where it runs on —
    and where the metric degenerates (a sphere's pole, a cone's apex). The
    start, direction and length may use sliders, t and named points, so
    dragging P moves a `geodesic(S, P, …)`; a list draws a fan:
    `a = [0..11] pi/6` and `geodesic(S, (0, 0), (cos(a), sin(a)))`. It must be
    the whole row. A fan of very long geodesics shares a fixed amount of
    work, so its members may end short of the length asked for; the row's
    note then says so ("cut short at L ≈ 472 of 1000"). On a sphere
    they are great circles, on a cylinder helices,
    on a plane straight lines; on a surface of revolution r cos ψ is constant
    along one (Clairaut).
  - On a panel drawn on a surface, `geodesic((x0, y0), (dx, dy))` (or
    `geodesic(P, (dx, dy), L)`) draws on that surface, in the panel's x and
    y, and runs on across x and y's ranges where the surface repeats. Drag P
    along the surface to move it.
- Metrics: a row `ds^2 = …` (or `ds² = …`) gives a plane panel its own
  metric, a quadratic form in differentials `d<name>`, and `geodesic` and
  `lightray` rows in that panel follow it. Only in that row is `dr` the
  differential of r; elsewhere names starting with d keep their meaning.
  - The differentials are those of the panel's two coordinates — `dx` and
    `dy`, or of two coordinates defined from x and y (`r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2)`,
    `phi = atan2(y, x)`) — and of at most one more, a time no component
    depends on. Coefficients are any expressions in x, y, those coordinates
    and sliders; cross terms (`2 a dt dphi`) are allowed:
    `ds^2 = (dx^2 + dy^2)/y^2` (the Poincaré half-plane) or `M = 1`,
    `ds^2 = -(1 - 2M/r) dt^2 + dr^2/(1 - 2M/r) + r^2 dphi^2` (Schwarzschild,
    in its equatorial plane). Define r and phi first: `dr` and `dphi` with
    no such coordinates are refused. Inside ds² `dt` (or `dτ`, `dtau`) is
    a differential even beside a slider named dt, dτ or τ; another defined
    name like `dw` keeps its value there. A component using t (or τ, when
    dτ is the time) is refused
    (time-dependent metrics are not supported yet), as is one using the
    extra coordinate, a missing differential of the panel's coordinates, two
    extra coordinates, `dpi` or `de` (constants are no coordinates), a term
    not quadratic in the differentials, and a metric with no usable
    signature (checked over scales from 0.001 to 100 000 round the origin):
    with no extra coordinate it must be positive definite (a plane) or
    Lorentzian, det g < 0 (a spacetime diagram, below), somewhere, and may
    be both (mixed signature, read out as such: each geodesic takes the
    kind at its start and stops where it changes, the row's note saying
    "stops where the metric stops being Lorentzian (a plane beyond)" or
    the reverse; negative for every
    direction is refused); with one, the panel's
    coordinates are space and det g < 0, so the other is a time.
    One ds² row a panel; not on an `on(…)` panel or one whose `view(…)` maps
    its axes. The row reads out its signature and coordinates and draws
    nothing.
  - Points and directions are in the panel's x and y, like any point (named
    points drag); the metric is pulled back to x and y through the
    coordinates' Jacobian, and the curve is drawn there.
  - With no time coordinate, `geodesic(P, (dx, dy))` runs at unit speed; a
    third argument is its length in the metric. Poincaré's geodesics are
    half-circles on y = 0: from (0, 1) along (1, 0), the unit circle.
  - In a spacetime, `geodesic(P, (vx, vy))` is a massive particle: (vx, vy)
    is its coordinate velocity d(x, y)/dt, so its size matters — round
    Schwarzschild with M = 1, `geodesic((10, 0), (0, sqrt(1/10)))` is a
    circular orbit — and the length is proper time. Faster than light at P
    draws nothing and the row's note says how fast it may go ("faster than
    light here: at most ≈ 0.894 in this direction"). A spinning hole works
    too (equatorial Kerr, with a `dt dphi` term): geodesics run on into the
    ergoregion, where g_tt > 0 and nothing can stand still, down to the
    horizon.
  - `lightray(P, (dx, dy))` is a light ray: only the direction matters, and
    its length runs in the affine parameter that moves like t at the start.
    `b = [-6..6]` and `lightray((-30, b), (1, 0))` bend round a black hole;
    those with |b| < 3√3 M fall in.
  - Without a length they run until they leave a box round the window (four
    times its size, kept through small pans and zooms, and grown to take in
    the start, so a ray sent in from far off still crosses a zoomed window)
    or have drawn as far as that is across. They stop where the metric
    degenerates or blows up — a horizon (r = 2M), an ideal boundary
    (y = 0) — and lists fan out as for surfaces. Orbits precess as they
    should: 2π((1 − 6M/r)^−½ − 1) an orbit near a circle of radius r.
  - A spacetime diagram: with no third coordinate, a Lorentzian metric in
    the panel's own two (one minus sign) makes the panel space against time,
    and the metric decides which is which: `ds^2 = -dy^2 + dx^2`
    (Minkowski, y up as time), `g = 0.1` and `ds^2 = -(1 + 2 g x) dy^2 +
    dx^2` (a uniform field: a plane where 1 + 2 g x < 0), `M = 1` and
    `ds^2 = -(1 - 2M/x) dy^2 + dx^2/(1 - 2M/x)` (Schwarzschild's r and t
    as x and y), `ds^2 = -(1 - 2M/x) dy^2 + 2 dy dx` (ingoing
    Eddington–Finkelstein, r and v). Declared coordinates work as above.
    `geodesic(P, (vx, vy))` is a particle whose coordinate direction is
    (vx, vy), normalised to proper time (the length); it must point inside
    the light cone, else the note says "v must point inside the light cone
    here". `lightray(P, (dx, dy))` runs along the null direction nearest
    (dx, dy) by angle in x and y — one of four, the two null lines either
    way, so `(1, 1)` and `(-1, 1)` are the two future rays in Minkowski
    and any direction picks one wherever P is dragged; its length is an
    affine parameter, distance in the panel at the start. They stop where
    the metric degenerates or blows up, or the coordinates freeze (a
    particle falling toward r = 2M in Schwarzschild's t only creeps up the
    line x = 2M; in Eddington–Finkelstein it crosses and stops at r → 0).
  - `gaussian(x, y)` alone on a row is the metric's Gaussian curvature K,
    painted over the panel on the diverging scale of a surface's (row colour
    where K > 0, its complement where K < 0, nothing at 0), scaled to the
    90th percentile of |K| over the view (but at least a thousandth of its
    largest), and read on hover where no curve or point is near. Where K is
    only rounding (a flat metric) nothing is painted and hover reads 0.
    `-gaussian(x, y)` and `c gaussian(x, y)` (c a number or slider) are
    shaded to their own size too. `gaussian(P)` or `gaussian(0.3, 2)` is the
    number at a point. K comes from the metric alone (Brioschi's formula, from g and its
    first and second derivatives), taken in the coordinates it is written
    in — r and phi, say — and then written in x and y (K is a scalar). The
    Poincaré half-plane `(dx^2 + dy^2)/y^2` and disk
    `4(dx^2 + dy^2)/(1 - x^2 - y^2)^2` have K = −1 everywhere, the
    stereographic sphere `4(dx^2 + dy^2)/(1 + x^2 + y^2)^2` +1,
    `dr^2 + sin(r)^2 dphi^2` +1, `dr^2 + r^2 dphi^2` 0 (painted nothing).
    `meancurvature` needs a surface in space and is refused here.
  - With a time, `gaussian(x, y)` is the curvature of space at one instant:
    K of the slice t = constant, whose metric is g's spatial block (cross
    terms like dt dphi do not reach it). Schwarzschild's slice
    `dr^2/(1 - 2M/r) + r^2 dphi^2` is Flamm's paraboloid's: K = −M/r³. It
    is left unpainted where the slice is not space (inside the horizon).
  - On a spacetime diagram (a Lorentzian ds² in x and y alone),
    `gaussian(x, y)` is K = R/2, half the scalar curvature (Brioschi's K is
    R₁₂₁₂/det g for any signature): `-(1 - 2M/x) dy^2 + dx^2/(1 - 2M/x)`
    has K = 2M/r³, Rindler `-x^2 dy^2 + dx^2` 0, de Sitter's static patch
    `-(1 - x^2/L^2) dy^2 + dx^2/(1 - x^2/L^2)` +1/L², anti-de Sitter's
    −1/L². It is painted where the metric is Lorentzian (and, of mixed
    signature, where it is positive definite: the plane's K there), and
    left out where it degenerates.
- Light cones: `lightcones` alone on a row draws the light cones of its
  panel's ds² metric on a lattice over the window (spaced like a tensor
  field's glyphs, a power of two near 56 px, and fixed in the plane as it
  pans); `lightcone(P)` draws one at a point (P drags; a list of points
  draws one each). Refused with no metric, or a Riemannian one.
  - On a spacetime diagram each is the two null directions, a filled wedge
    opening to the future and two strokes to the past, a fixed size on the
    screen, only where the metric is Lorentzian. The future is the half
    along which the time coordinate increases, and the time coordinate is
    the one the row writes as such: that of the first term (left to right)
    that is a squared differential carrying a minus sign — subtracted, or
    with a unary minus or negative number among its factors; a sum factor
    holding differentials is split into its terms (`s (-dx^2 + dy^2)`,
    `(dy^2 - dx^2)/x^2`), and `dx dx` and `(dx/c)^2` are squares, while a
    sign inside a factor that is a plain value, like (1 - 2M/x), does not
    count. With no such term, the coordinate whose own d²-term is negative
    wherever the metric is Lorentzian, else y. So
    `-(1 - 2M/x) dy^2 + dx^2/(1 - 2M/x)` and `dx^2 - f dy^2` have time y,
    `-dx^2 + dy^2` and `-(1 - 2M/y) dx^2 + 2 dx dy` have time x, and
    `2 dx dy` alone has y; it never changes as sliders move. That is
    continuous wherever that coordinate is a time, inside a horizon too.
    Where the cone lies across it exactly (inside Schwarzschild's horizon in
    r and t, where r is the time) the future is the other coordinate
    decreasing: smaller r. Round a horizon in
    Schwarzschild's r and t the cones close up (half-angle
    atan(1 − 2M/r)); in Eddington–Finkelstein they tip over through it.
  - With a time besides the panel's coordinates (equatorial Schwarzschild
    or Kerr in r and phi) each is the light-speed ellipse: the coordinate
    velocities v = d(x, y)/dt light can have, g_tt + 2 g_ti vⁱ + g_ij vⁱ vʲ
    = 0, drawn round a dot at its point at one scale for the whole panel
    (a power of two, so that the median ellipse in view reaches about a
    third of a lattice cell): each is where light from its dot gets in the
    same short time. Flat space gives circles centred on their dots; round
    Schwarzschild at r, 1 − 2M/r across and √(1 − 2M/r) round, shrinking
    toward the horizon (nothing inside it); round a spinning hole they are
    dragged in its sense of spin, and inside the ergoregion (g_tt > 0) an
    ellipse no longer holds its own dot. A lattice ellipse wider than its
    cell is left out, and so is one cut off from the outside by a horizon
    (inside a spinning hole's inner horizon, where x and y are space
    again) — unless every way out meets a horizon (de Sitter's cosmological
    one), when none is. A lone `lightcone(P)` with no ellipse in view on the lattice is
    drawn at its own such scale.
- Tidal forces: `tidal` alone on a row draws what the panel's ds² metric
  does to a small cloud of free particles held at rest, on the same lattice
  as light cones; `tidal(P)` draws it at a point (P drags; a list of points
  draws one each). The observer is static, moving along the time
  coordinate (u = ∂t/√(−g_tt)), and its tidal tensor E_ij = R_iαjβ u^α u^β
  gives the separation ξ of two nearby particles ξ'' = −E ξ. Each glyph is
  two crossed bars along E's eigenvectors (in the panel's x and y), half as
  long as |λ| times one scale for the panel (a power of two, so the median
  glyph in view reaches about a fifth of a lattice cell; kept as you pan
  while the median allows, taken afresh when a slider moves), with
  arrowheads pointing out where it stretches (λ < 0) and in where it
  squeezes (λ > 0). One stronger than its cell
  allows is shrunk whole, keeping its shape. Round Schwarzschild
  (`-(1 - 2M/r) dt^2 + dr^2/(1 - 2M/r) + r^2 dphi^2`) λ = −2M/r³ along the
  radius and +M/r³ round, exactly; Reissner–Nordström −2M/r³ + 3Q²/r⁴ and
  M/r³ − Q²/r⁴; de Sitter's static patch −1/L² both ways; flat space draws
  nothing. There is no glyph where no observer can stand still (g_tt ≥ 0:
  inside a horizon, or a spinning hole's ergoregion, where g_tφ drags
  everything round), nor behind a horizon (as for light cones). Cross terms
  are taken into account: space is h_ij = g_ij − g_ti g_tj/g_tt. Riemann
  comes from symbolic first and second derivatives of g in the coordinates
  it is written in (r and phi), so a metric flat in polar coordinates is
  exactly flat.
  - On a spacetime diagram (a Lorentzian ds² in x and y alone) there is one
    direction of space and one bar: λ = −K = −R/2 for any observer, along
    the direction orthogonal to the written time coordinate's ∂τ (the one
    light cones take as time) — −2M/r³ in Schwarzschild's r and t.
  - Refused with no metric, or a Riemannian one: tidal forces need a time,
    so write the ds² with a dt term.
- Derivatives: `d/dx (x^3)` differentiates symbolically; higher order
  `d^2/dx^2 (...)`; works for any single-letter variable, e.g. `d/dq (q^2)`.
  The operand is every factor written after `dx`, with or without spaces,
  up to the next operator or closing bracket: `d/dx x sin(x)` is the
  derivative of x sin(x), while `d/dx x^3/x` is 3x²/x, `d/dx x * x` is
  1·x, and `(d/dx x^2) x` is 2x·x.
  Along x, y, or z it works through lists too: with `N = [1..4]`,
  `y = d/dx x^N` is a family of curves, and `y = d/dx [sin(x), x^2]` draws
  `y = cos(x)` and `y = 2x`.
  Along t a named list is refused (its elements may use t).
- Sums and products: `sum(n=1..N, sin(n x)/n)` and `prod(k=1..N, k)`, also
  written `Σ`/`Π`. The bracket form `sum[n=1..N] sin(n x)/n` takes everything
  after it in the product chain as the body (`2 sum[n=1..N] ...` keeps the 2
  outside). Bounds must be numbers or constants defined in another row (not
  `t`), because the sum is expanded symbolically before compiling — which makes
  `N` a slider that adds terms as you drag it. A bound may also be a named
  list of numbers: with `N = [3..5]`, `y = sum(n=1..N, sin(n x)/n)` draws one
  partial sum per element (a family that pairs with other uses of `N`).
  Inside a sum over `n`, a sequence term `a_n` is each term: `sum(n=1..N, a_n)`.
- Integrals: `int[a..b] f(x) dx` (definite) and `int(f(x) dx)`
  (antiderivative), also written `∫`. The trailing `dx` names the variable;
  any letter works, so `y = int[0..x] exp(-t^2) dt` plots a function of x,
  and bounds may use sliders, t, or x. Integration is symbolic where a
  verified antiderivative exists — polynomials and rational functions
  (exactly), the elementary families, u-substitution, integration by parts,
  Gaussians via erf — and falls back to Gauss–Legendre quadrature expanded
  in place otherwise, so non-elementary rows like `y = int[0..x] sin(t)/t dt`
  (Si) still plot. A row whose integral resolves to a constant shows the
  numeric value as a readout — and when the row is exactly one definite
  integral of a real integrand (`int[0..b] sin(x) dx`; bounds may be sliders,
  states, t or `±inf`), it also shades the area between the integrand and the
  axis over [a, b], in 2D: parts that add to the value in the row color,
  parts that subtract in its complement (so reversed bounds swap the tints).
  The dx variable runs along the horizontal axis whatever its letter; add
  `y = sin(x)` as its own row to see the curve beyond [a, b]. A coefficient,
  a sum of integrals, an iterated integral or a definition
  (`A = int[0..1] x^2 dx`) stays a plain number. Classic notations work: `int[0..1] dx/(1+x^2)`,
  and iterated integrals pair inside-out: `int[0..1] int[0..y] x dx dy`.
  Bounds may be `±inf` (or `∞`): `int[-inf..x] exp(t) dt` is exp(x),
  `int[-inf..inf] exp(-x^2) dx` reads √π, and `int[-inf..x] normalpdf(t, 0, 1) dt`
  is the normal cdf. Divergent limits are refused (the closed form is checked
  against real quadrature), not misreported.
- Lists: `[3, 1, 4]`, or ranges `[1..20]`, `[0, 0.5..10]` (the first two
  elements set the step), `[10..1]` (counts down). Range bounds are numbers
  or constants defined in another row, like Σ bounds. List math broadcasts
  elementwise — `2L + 1`, `sin(L)`, `L^2`. A list is a variable that ranges
  over its values: the row is evaluated once per instance, so every use of
  the SAME list moves together (zips) — `s = [1..50]/5` then `(s, sin(s))`
  is a scatter of samples, and lists derived from `s` (`q = s^2`,
  `s[s > 2]`, `a_[s]`) stay paired with it. Lists with DIFFERENT origins are
  independent and cross: each `[…]` literal is its own origin, so
  `([0,1],[0,1],[0,1])` is the 8 corners of a cube, `[1,2] + [10,20,30]` has
  6 elements, and two separately defined lists `(a, b)` make a grid. Columns
  of one data file share its rows, so `(data.x, data.y)` pairs up. To pair
  literal values write the points out: `P = [(1,4), (2,5), (3,6)]`; then
  `P.x` and `P.y` (and `P.z`) are the lists of their coordinates, paired the
  same way — `(P.x, 2 P.y)` is 3 points, not 9. Brackets add: a list
  inside a list contributes its elements, so with `n = [1,2]`, `[n, 3, 5]`
  is `[1, 2, 3, 5]` (a new list, independent of `n`). A bracket around one
  item is that item: `[n]` is `n` (so `n + [n]` has 2 elements, like
  `n + n`), and `[x + 1] 2` groups.
  `[]` is the empty list: combined with anything it gives `[]`, and
  `count([])` and `total([])` are 0.
- Cases over a list decide each element: `{L > 2: L}` with `L = [1..4]` is
  `[3, 4]`, and an element no case holds for (with no otherwise) is not in
  the list at all, so `count({L > 2: L})` is 2. A whole point goes at once,
  and over lists a case may test equality. A function's point parameters
  read coordinates as `p.x`, `p.y`, `p.z`: `c(p, q) = {p.y = q.x: (p.x,
  q.y)}` composes arrows i → j and j → k, and with lists of arrows `A`, `B`,
  `AB = c(A, B)` is the arrows that meet (their matrix product, as a multiset
  of arrows), and `c(A, A)` pairs each arrow with itself: one name is one
  choice. Two independent draws from one list are binders, rows of their
  own: `p ∈ A` (or `p \in A`) names a choice from A, equal to A but never
  identical, so with `p ∈ A` and `q ∈ A`, `c(p, q)` is A composed with
  itself (`p + p` still zips; `p + q` crosses). A binder cannot use a name
  the language has: x, y, z, t, u, v, w, d, e, i, pi, a name starting
  u_, or a built-in function such as sin. A binder draws members, not a
  range: `a ∈ [0, 10]` is 0 or 10; every number from 0 to 10 is
  `a = interval(0, 10)`, and the whole numbers are `a ∈ [0..10]`.
- List reductions: `mean(L)`, `total(L)`, `count(L)`, `min(L)`, `max(L)`,
  `stdev(L)` (sample), `median(L)`. A row that reduces to a
  constant shows the numeric value as a readout. mean/total/count/min/max
  expand symbolically, so elements may animate (`mean([sin(t), 2])`);
  stdev/median/sort need constant elements. A function applies to one
  member of a list argument at a time, a reduction in its body included:
  with `f(m) = total(L m)`, `f(M)` is one total per member of M (and
  `total(f(M))` their total), a number reduces as its one member (`mean(5)`
  is 5), so a wrapper `avg(s) = mean(s)` gives `avg(L)` = L back: reduce
  a list in the row, `mean(L)`. Over a list of points the body reads `p.x`,
  `p.y`. Over a column, a missing cell is
  left out of every reduction (as it is of `hist`) except `count(L)`, which
  answers how many rows there are.
- `hist(L)` bins a list into a bar chart — `hist(L, 40)` sets the bin count
  (default ≈ √n, between 5 and 60). It is a whole row, not a value, and the
  one thing you may do to it is scale it: the plane has a single scale for
  both axes, so counts in the thousands need `hist(L, 40) / 800` to share a
  view with values in the units. Missing values are left out.
- Order lives in tuples. A list `[ … ]` has no order — `[3, 1, 2]` and
  `[1, 2, 3]` are the same list — so anything that needs one takes a tuple
  `( … )`. `sort(L)` is L's values in ascending order, as a tuple, and
  `sort(P, key)` orders a list by a key written in that list: `sort(P, P.x)`,
  `sort((s, sin(s)), s)`. A tuple of 2 or 3 numbers is a point
  (`sort([3, 1, 2])` draws the point (1, 2, 3)); a longer one reads out,
  `sort([5, 3, 8, 1, 2])` = (1, 2, 3, 5, 8), and draws nothing. Tuples of one
  length combine position by position, like vectors: `sort(A) + sort(B)`. A
  tuple of points, `T = ((0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 0))`, is one value in order —
  `polyline(T)` walks it — and a square one is also a matrix.
- Indexing is 1-based and needs a tuple: with `T = sort([7, 5, 6])` in a row
  above, `T[2]` is 6 and `T[k]` takes k from a slider. `T[2..3]` is (6, 7),
  and a list of indices picks one element each: `T[[3, 1]]` is `[7, 5]`, and
  `T[N]` for a named list `N` pairs with `N`. `L[2]` on a list `[ … ]` is an
  error that says to sort it first; a filter `L[L > 2]` is no index and
  works on any list. A named tuple or list indexes, and so does a sort
  call, `sort(L)[2]`; `x[2]` is plain multiplication (2x) for any other
  name. On a list of points or tuples, which has no k-th element, `[k]` is
  position k of each: with `A = [(1, 1), (1, 2)]`, `A[1]` is `A.x`, paired
  with `A.y`, and `Q[4]` is the 4th entry of every 4-tuple in Q. `.x`,
  `.y`, `.z` name the coordinates of a point (2 or 3 of them), on one named
  point too (`P.x`); a longer tuple is read by position only. A function's
  parameters index (`c(p) = p[4]`), and tuple arguments arrive whole when
  they fill the parameters: `c((3, 12, 6, 2))`, `c((1, 2), (3, 4))`. A
  recursive function's parameters are numbers: pass a point's coordinates.
- Data columns: with `person = open("people.csv", 3a7f9c1d2e4b)` in a row
  above (see Definitions), `person.age` is a list of that column's numbers.
  Everything lists can do applies: `(person.age, person.height)` is a
  scatter, `mean(person.age)` a readout. File order is not part of the
  data: each record's position in the file is `person.row` (`row_index`
  when the file has its own `row` column), so `sort(person.age, person.row)`
  is the column in file order, and
  `polyline(sort((person.x, person.y), person.row))` draws a series in it
  (or sort by the x column itself). Naming
  works throughout — `half = person.age / 2`, `P = (person.age, person.height)`
  — and a named scatter is still a scatter. Only the
  device that dropped the file has its data — the link carries the file's
  name and hash, not its bytes.
- A comparison over a list keeps the members it holds for: `L > 2` (or
  `L[L > 2]`) is the elements above 2, `count(L > 2)` how many. It keeps
  members of the list, not the values compared: `L^2 < 4` keeps elements
  of L, `P.x < 0` keeps points of P. Inside `{…}` a comparison is still one
  condition per element: `{L > 2: 1, 0}`. Index by a comparison to choose
  one column by another: `person.height[person.age >= 18]` (rows stay
  aligned), chains, `person.age[30 <= person.age < 40]`, and text,
  `person.height[person.city == "NYC"]` (`!=` too, and either quote).
  Filtering a whole file names a new one,
  `adults = person[person.age >= 18]`, whose columns work like any others
  (`(adults.age, adults.height)`). A filter settles when the row compiles, so
  it may use constants and sliders but not t; a comparison with a missing
  cell is false, so filtering also drops gaps.
- Text columns are lists of text. They are not plottable and have no
  arithmetic directly. `person.name.length` returns a numeric list of character
  counts (Unicode code points) and plots one count per row. Missing cells stay
  gaps; counts use the parsed, trimmed text. Use it in arithmetic, reductions,
  histograms, and filters: `hist(person.name.length)` or
  `long_names = person[person.name.length > 10]`. `count(person.name)` still
  counts rows. `==` and `!=` exist only for filters: an equation still takes
  a single `=`.
- Comments: a row starting with `#` (e.g. `# tangent lines`) plots nothing; in
  the app it renders as a heading whose group (the rows until the next `#` row)
  can be collapsed. Use them to label sections of longer documents.
- Notes: `#` after a row's math starts a note to the end of the row
  (`y = x^2 # parabola`, `a = 2 # slope`). Only the math before it is read;
  the app shows the note in small text under the row. A `;` still ends the
  row, note included.
- Row colors: a note that opens with a hex color draws the row in that color
  (`y = x^2 #e24`, `y = sin(x) #1f77b4 wave`). The 3 or 6 hex digits must
  touch the `#`; `# 100 samples` (with a space) stays a plain note. Without
  one, the rows that draw take the palette in order (blue, red, green,
  purple, orange, black); definitions, comments and view rows take no color.

## Variables (what a row means)

- `x`, `y`: the 2D plane. `y = f(x)`, or any implicit equation in x and y
  (`x^2+y^2=4`), renders as a curve. A row is drawn per pixel when it
  depends on x or y, so a bare expression like `sin(x)` is a scalar field,
  not a curve: write `y = sin(x)` for the graph.
- `z`: using z switches to 3D. `z = sin(x)cos(y)` is a surface;
  `x^2+y^2+z^2=9` is an implicit 3D surface. A bare expression in x, y, z is
  a field in space, drawn as a translucent cloud (see Scalar field); write
  `… = 0` for its surface.
- `t`: time in seconds. Any row mentioning `t` animates, e.g.
  `y = sin(x - 2t)`.
- `u`, `v`: the parametric parameters, two intervals (below) that are
  `u = interval(0, 1)` and `v = interval(0, 1)` unless a row redefines them
  as another: with `u = interval(0, 2pi)`, `(cos(u), sin(u))` is the whole
  circle. A row whose value is a point traces curves and surfaces, however
  it is written: `(u, u^2)`, `(0,0,1) u` and `u e_z` are all curves; a
  complex expression in u alone is a path (`exp(i 2 pi u)`). A bare real row
  in u and v alone draws the values it takes as a density curve: `u^2` has
  density 1/(2√x), `u v` has −ln(x).
- `interval(a, b)`: every real number from a to b (a < b; the bounds may use
  sliders and t). `[1..2]` is only the whole numbers 1 and 2. Every mention
  of one name is the same number, so with `r = interval(1, 2)`, `r + r` is
  2r; each written `interval(…)` is a separate one, so
  `interval(0, 1) + interval(0, 1)` is the sum of two. In a tuple it traces
  with u and v:
  `(r cos(2 pi u), r sin(2 pi u))` is a filled annulus, `(r, r^2)` a curve
  over [1, 2]. With a list it crosses into one curve per member, as u does:
  `(interval(0, 1), 0) + (0, [1, 2])` is two segments, at heights 1 and 2.
  A row in x and y over one interval is a family, drawn as the
  region its members sweep: with `a = interval(1, 2)`, `y = sin(a x)` shades
  every point some a from 1 to 2 puts on its curve, and `y < a x` every point
  below some member. At most one interval in such a row, and a bare field
  (`sin(a x)`) is an error: set it equal to something. Alone, an interval row
  draws its values against length: `interval(0, 10)` is the line at height 1
  over [0, 10].
- Reductions over continuous sets are integrals: `count` is the measure,
  `total` the integral, `mean` their ratio. Over u, v and intervals the
  measure is length: `total(u^2)` is 1/3, `count(interval(1, 3))` is 2,
  `count((u, u^2))` is 1 (a parametric set carries its parameter's length).
  Over x (all of ℝ) `total(exp(-x^2))` is √π, `count(x)` is ∞, and a total
  that does not converge is an error. A filter is the set it keeps, measured
  in its own dimension: `count(x^2 + y^2 < 1)` is the area π,
  `count(x^2 + y^2 = 1)` the length 2π, `count(x^2 = 2)` the 2 roots; other
  reductions take its members, so `total(0 < x < 1)` is 1/2 (a region's
  members are points: use `count` for its area). Reduce
  a value over a set with `{conditions: value}`, the conditions joined by
  "and" (only here may one be an equation): `total({x^2 + y^2 < 1: x y})`,
  `mean({y = x^2, 0 < x < 1: y})`. The measure depends on the set, not the
  spelling (`2y = 2x^2` agrees with `y = x^2`), and never on the view: an
  unbounded region counts ∞, and a count of roots that cannot all be found
  (`sin(x) = 0`) is an error — restrict it, `count({-10 < x < 10, sin(x) = 0})`.
  `min`/`max` work over u, v and intervals and over points; `stdev`,
  `median` and `hist` of a continuous set, sets in space (x, y, z) and totals
  over unbounded plane regions are errors. A list in the argument keeps the
  list reduction: with `L = [1, 2, 3]`, `y = total(L x)` is the line y = 6x.
- `w`: the complex plane point x + iy. A complex-valued expression in `w`
  (e.g. `ln(w-2) - ln(w+2)`) draws field lines and equipotentials. Wrapping it
  in `domain(…)` or `conformal(…)` picks a different view of the same function.
- `z` inside `iter(…)`: the iterate being fed back through the step. Outside
  `iter`, `z` is the 3D axis as above.

## Row types

- Curve: an equation in x and y — `y = x^2`, `(x^2+y^2)^2 = 8(x^2-y^2)`.
- Region: inequalities, including chains — `y < x/2 + 1`,
  `4 <= x^2 + y^2 <= 9`. Non-strict comparisons draw a solid boundary.
- Scalar field: a bare expression in x and/or y — `sin(x)cos(y)`, or `sin(x)`
  (constant along y) — shaded by value: the row color where it is positive,
  the color's complement where negative, stronger the larger it is. There is
  no implicit graph; a row in x alone reads out how to write its curve
  (`y = sin(x)`). A list of fields (`a = [1, 2]; sin(a x)`) is an error: write
  `y = sin(a x)` for the curves.
- Scalar field in space: a bare expression in x, y and z — `x y z`,
  `z exp(-sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)/2)` — is a translucent cloud, tinted the same
  way (row color positive, complement negative) and denser where the field is
  larger. The density is relative: the scale is what |f| typically reaches in
  the view, so `x y z` and a tiny orbital both show, and a slider that only
  multiplies the field changes nothing. The cloud fills a soft ball around
  the view's center, fading out before the camera; a field that dies away
  (an orbital) shows whole, and zooming out shows more of one that does not
  (`x y z`). An implicit surface in the same
  graph is seen through the cloud in front of it, so
  `f(x, y, z) = …; f(x, y, z); f(x, y, z) = 0.5` draws a level surface inside
  its field. For nested level surfaces instead, write
  `f(x, y, z) = [1..5]`.
- Value: a bare expression with no plot coordinate — `2+2`, `sqrt(a)` with a
  slider a, `|A - B|` between named points, `int[0..1] x^2 dx`, `sin(t)` —
  draws nothing (a lone definite integral shades its area) and reads out `= 4` (or `≈ 1.41421`) under the row, live as
  sliders, states and t move. The tool result reports it as kind `value`
  with the number in `value`. A number is not assumed to mean `y = number`:
  write `y = 4` for the horizontal line.
- Complex point: a constant complex expression such as `1+2i` draws at (1, 2).
  Constants and t may animate its real and imaginary components. A named
  one, `a = e^(i pi/3)`, is written in wherever `a` is read (`a^2`,
  `domain(w - a)`, `[1..|a|]`), and a real value reached through complex
  ones is a constant like any other (`b = re(a)`, `r = |3 + 4i|`).
- Complex list: one complex member makes a list complex — `1` in
  `[1, i, -1]` is 1 + 0i — and it draws each member as a complex point:
  `n = 5; e^(2 pi i [0..n-1]/n)` is the fifth roots of unity, n on a
  slider. Name it like any list (`S = e^(i pi [0..5]/5)`); `re(S)`,
  `abs(S)` and `(re(S), im(S))` are real. `total`, `mean` and `count`
  reduce it; `sort`, `median`, `stdev`, `min`, `max` and `hist` need real
  numbers, so take `abs`, `re` or `im` first (filters and sort keys too:
  `S[re(S) > 0]`; equality needs neither, `S[S == 1]`). `sort(S, re(S))`
  is S's members in order, a tuple, which has no picture yet: `T[k]` picks
  one. Members are drawn split into
  real and imaginary parts, 2^21 nodes in all: constant members are two
  numbers each, but thousands of members of a slider-dependent polynomial
  are too many. A list cannot mix complex numbers with points, and a
  point's coordinates stay real (`(S, 1)` is an error).
- Complex roots: `w^3 = 1` draws three solution points; equations in w become
  two real constraints. This is a numerical search over the visible window,
  with exact labels for rational/quadratic polynomial factors and a defining-
  polynomial label for remaining algebraic roots. The optional certification
  control proves completeness only when every region in its search box is settled.
- Complex path: a complex-valued expression whose only variable is u (constants,
  sliders and t aside) draws the path it traces over u, at
  (re, im) — the same plane as complex points and roots. `exp(i 2 pi u)` is
  the unit circle; with `f(w) = w^2 + w`, `f(exp(i 2 pi u))` is its image
  under f. Supported: arithmetic, powers, exp ln log sqrt, sin cos tan sinh
  cosh tanh, re im abs arg conj, user functions. Branch cuts (`sqrt`, `ln`,
  fractional powers) break the curve where the value jumps. An equation,
  inequality, or a use of v is an error, as is a path whose split into real
  and imaginary parts is too large (deeply nested products). An expression
  that mentions i but is real for every u (`abs(exp(i u))`) is not a path
  and says so.
- Complex plot: a complex expression in `w` — `w + 4/w`.
- RGB color field: `rgb(red, green, blue)` fills the 2D plane with a color at
  each (x, y). Channels are real expressions on the 0–1 scale (not CSS's
  0–255); values outside that range are clamped, so `rgb(255, 128, 0)` is
  white, not orange. `rgb(1, 0, 0)` fills the plane red. Expressions may
  use x, y, t, sliders, coordinate fields, and real projections of w such as
  `arg(w)` or `abs(w)`. For example,
  `rgb(cos(arg(w)/2)^2, cos(arg(w)/2+1)^2, cos(arg(w)/2+2)^2)`.
  This is a whole-row plot mode, not a color value for styling another row;
  it cannot be nested in arithmetic or lists and does not take u, v, or z.
  A pixel with any undefined or infinite channel is transparent, so a partial
  piecewise channel can restrict the field: `rgb({x>0:1}, 0, 0)`. An
  optional fourth argument is the opacity, 0–1 (clamped; default 1), so a
  field can fade into the graph paper: `rgb(1, 0, 0, exp(-x^2-y^2))`.
  RGB, HSL and OKLCH rows share the same layer and draw in row order;
  curves and regions draw over them.
  Static share-card previews use the site card; the live graph renders the field.
- HSL color field: `hsl(hue, saturation, lightness)` uses hue in radians and
  saturation/lightness on a 0–1 scale (not CSS's percentages). Hue wraps
  around 2pi; saturation/lightness are clamped. `hsl(2pi/3, 1, 0.5)` is
  green. An animated wheel is `hsl(arg(w)+t/3, 1, 0.5)`.
- OKLCH color field: `oklch(lightness, chroma, hue)` uses lightness 0–1,
  nonnegative chroma (typically 0–0.4), and hue in radians. Lightness is
  clamped, negative chroma becomes zero and hue wraps around 2pi. Zero chroma
  is neutral gray; lightness 0 and 1 give black and white. Colors outside
  sRGB are mapped by reducing chroma at fixed lightness and hue, then encoded
  as sRGB. This is strict chroma reduction, not CSS's local-MINDE algorithm
  or wide-gamut output. Try `oklch(0.72, 0.16, arg(w)+t/3)` for a wheel
  with more even perceived lightness than HSL. HSL and OKLCH have the same
  real-channel, whole-row and transparency rules as RGB; all three accept
  equations, sliders and time. Every channel is 0–1 except hue (radians,
  like trig functions and `arg`, so `arg(w)` is a hue directly) and chroma.
  To port a CSS color, divide 0–255 channels by 255, percentages by 100, and
  write a degree hue as `h pi/180`.
- Domain coloring: `domain(f)` where f is complex — `domain(w^2 + 1)`. Hue is
  arg f, brightness |f|; zeros render black and poles white.
- Conformal map: `conformal(f)` — `conformal(w^2/4)` — draws the image of the
  coordinate grid under f (the level curves of re f and im f).
- Fractal: `iter(step)` iterates `z ↦ step`, coloring by escape time. Inside
  `iter` only, `z` is the iterate. If the step mentions the plane (`w`, `x`,
  `y`) iteration starts at 0, so `iter(z^2 + w)` is the Mandelbrot set; with a
  fixed constant the pixel is the starting point, so `iter(z^2 - 0.8 + 0.156i)`
  is a Julia set. An optional second argument sets the iteration count,
  `iter(z^2 + w, 600)` (default 250, max 5000). Any expression works:
  `iter((|re(z)| - i |im(z)|)^2 + w)` is the burning ship.
  `iter` is for the plane; an escape-time fractal in space (the Mandelbulb,
  a quaternion Julia set) is a recursive function — see "Recursive
  function" below.
- Point: `(2, 3)`; animate with t: `(2cos(t), 2sin(t))`.
- Data list: `[3, 1, 4, 4]` is a dot plot on the number line — a dot at each
  value on the x axis, copies stacked upward, so 4 has dots at (4, 1) and
  (4, 2). A list has no order, so no index is drawn (a sequence `a_n` does
  draw at n). Values closer than a dot's width at the current zoom share a
  column, so a long list (`sin(L)` for `L = [1..300]`, a CSV column of
  thousands) stacks into the shape of its distribution rather than one row of
  overlapping dots; zoom in and they separate. `[(1, 2), (3, 4)]` draws a
  scatter of points.
  Any list-valued expression plots the same way (`L^2 + 1`,
  `(L, L^2)` with `L` defined above, or a CSV column: `person.age`).
- Geometry: with points defined in rows above (`A = (0, 0)`), `segment(A, B)`,
  `polyline(A, B, C, …)` (an open path through the points, not filled),
  `vector(A, B)` (an arrow from A to B; `vector(V)` draws V from the origin —
  the head keeps its size on screen), `line(A, B)` (the infinite line through
  A and B), `polygon(A, B, C, …)` (filled), `square(A, B)` (erected on side A→B, to the left of the direction
  A→B), and `circle(center, radius)` draw figures that follow their points. Point arithmetic works anywhere: `A + B`, `2A`,
  `(A + B)/2`, `midpoint(A, B)`, `perp(A)` (rotate 90° counterclockwise),
  `rotate(P, a)` (turn by a about the origin; `rotate(P, a, C)` about C; in
  3D `rotate(P, a)` turns about z and `rotate(P, a, axis)` about axis),
  `unit(A)`, `dot(A, B)`, `cross(A, B)`, `|A - B|` (distance). Measurements:
  `distance(A, B)` is `|A - B|`; `angle(A, B, C)` is the angle at B, turning
  from B→A to B→C — signed, counterclockwise positive, in radians in (−π, π]
  (`angle(A, B, C) 180/pi` for degrees; wrap it in `abs(…)` for the unsigned
  angle) — and `angle(U, V)` is the same from vector U to vector V. Both are
  plain numbers: a bare row reads out "= value" (nothing is drawn — no arc
  marker), and they work inside any expression (`circle(A, distance(A, B))`).
  A scalar list inside a point broadcasts as in any scalar math
  (`distance(A, (L, 0))` is a list of distances); a list of points as an
  argument broadcasts too, and `T[1]` of a tuple of points selects one. An angle with a zero-length arm (`angle(A, A, C)`) reads "undefined". A parametric
  point like `A + u(B - A)` traces the segment. Tuple literals work directly
  as arguments (`segment((0, 0), A)`) and as operands: `A + (1, 2)`,
  `((0, 0) + B)/2`, `|(3, 4)|`.
- Geometry in space: `A = (1, 2, 3)` defines a 3D point with scalar
  components `A_x`, `A_y`, `A_z`. `segment`, `polyline`, `polygon`, and
  `vector` accept matching 2D or 3D points, including tuple literals. 3D
  triangles fill; larger 3D polygons draw their outline. `cross` returns a
  vector in 3D. 3D `angle` is unsigned in [0, pi]; zero arms are undefined.
  `line(A, B)` of 3D points is the infinite line through them, drawn across
  the view box. `perp`, `square`, and `circle` remain planar; 3D dragging is not defined.
  Point lists draw as dots in space too: `[0,1] e_x + [0,1] e_y` is 4 points,
  `[e_x, e_z]` 2, and `([0,1],[0,1],[0,1])` the 8 corners of a cube.
- Projective geometry (lines and planes as values): `join(A, B)` (or
  `line(A, B)`) is the line through two points, in the plane or in space;
  `join(A, B, C)` (or `plane(A, B, C)`) the plane through three points of
  space, and `plane(P, n)` the plane through P with normal n. `meet(L, M)`
  is where two lines of the plane cross, and in space where a line goes
  through a plane (a point) or two planes cross (a line); two lines of space
  do not meet. A meet is a point like any other — `X = meet(L, M)` names it,
  `polygon(meet(…), B, C)` and `midpoint(meet(…), A)` take it. Parallel
  lines meet at an ideal point, which draws nothing and reads out `at
  infinity, direction (1, 2)`. `project(P, L)` is the point of the line or
  plane L nearest P (or a line's shadow on a plane), and `reflect(P, L)`
  mirrors P in a line, a plane or a point. `distance(P, L)` measures from a
  point to a line or plane, and between lines or planes (0 where they cross);
  `angle(L, M)` is the acute angle between two lines or planes, in [0, π/2].
  A row holding a line or plane draws it — a line of the plane as its
  implicit line, a line of space across the view box, a plane as a surface —
  and reads out its equation: `= y = 2x + 1`, `= z = -x - y + 1`, or `=
  through (0, 0, 1), direction (1, 1, 0)` for a line of space. Name one
  (`L = join(A, B)`) to pass it on; the definition itself draws nothing, the
  row `L` does. A line or plane is no number or point, so `2 L` is an error.
  Lists broadcast as everywhere else: with `P = [A, B]`, `join(P, C)` is two
  lines, `L = join(P, C); meet(L, L)` pairs each line with itself, and
  `meet(K, H)` for a line K and a list of planes H is the list of crossing
  points, which `count`, `mean` and `total` take. A plane draws as a
  translucent sheet, outlined where it meets the view box, so a line in it
  or behind it shows through.
- Rigid motions (motors): `motor(L, th, d)` turns by th about the line L of
  space — right-handed about L's direction, A → B for `line(A, B)` — while
  sliding d along it (a screw; d may be left out); `motor(P, th)` turns the
  plane counterclockwise about the point P. `rotate(X, M)` moves a point, a
  list of points, a line, a plane or a figure by it:
  `rotate(hull(([0,1],[0,1],[0,1])), motor(line(A, B), t, t/4))` screws a
  cube along the axis through A and B, which stay draggable.
  `slerp(M1, M2, s)` is the rigid motion s of the way from M1 to M2, at
  constant speed along the screw between them — for motors that stay fixed
  (fixed axes, turns and slides), with the motion in s:
  `rotate(X, slerp(M1, M2, (1 - cos(t))/2))`. A row holding a motor draws
  its axis (or its centre, in the plane) and reads out what it does: `=
  turn 1.5708 about the line through (0, 0, 0), direction (0, 0, 1), slide
  2`, `turn 1.5708 about (1, 1)` or `slide (0, 0, 3)` — a motor and its
  opposite are one motion, read the shorter way round. A motor is no number
  or point: name it (`M = motor(L, t, 1)`) and pass it to rotate or slerp.
- Convex hulls: `hull(A, B, C, …)` or `hull(P)` for a whole point list draws
  the convex hull — a filled polygon in 2D, a lit opaque solid with flat-shaded faces and outlined edges in 3D
  (coplanar facets merge, so a cube shows six squares). Interior and repeated
  points are ignored, the points may move with sliders or t (the hull is
  rebuilt each frame), and flat 3D input degrades to a polygon. Up to 2000
  points in 3D. Point figures transform as a whole — `R hull(P)`,
  `2 polygon(A, B, C) + (1, 0)`, `-segment(A, B)`, `rotate(hull(P), a)`,
  `e^(t cross(n)) hull(P)` — meaning the figure of the transformed points
  (the same as `hull(R P)`; works for segment, polyline, polygon, vector and
  hull). A LIST in the transform draws one figure per element:
  `th = 2pi [0..4]/5; rotate(hull(P), th)` is a rosette of 5 hulls, while
  `hull(rotate(P, th))` is the single hull of all 5 copies. Point lists also
  transform on their own: `R P`, `P + (1, 0)`, `rotate(P, a)`.
  It composes with crossing lists and rotations:
  `hull(([0,1],[0,1],[0,1]))` is a solid cube, `hull(([-1,1],[-2,2]))` a
  rectangle, and `phi = (1+sqrt(5))/2; k = 2pi [0..2]/3;
  hull(rotate((0, [-1,1], [-phi,phi]), k, (1,1,1)))` a solid icosahedron.
- Object families: a list in a scalar position draws one object per element:
  `y = [1,2,3] x`, `circle((0,0), [1,2,3])`, `(cos(u),sin(u),[1,2,3])`.
  Uses of the same named list move together (`m = [1,2]`, `y = m x + m` is 2
  lines); independent lists cross (`y = [1,2] x + [0,1]` is 4 lines,
  `circle(([0,1],[0,1]), 1)` is 4 circles). Limit 32 objects, in 2D or 3D,
  or 8 implicit surfaces, curves of intersection or fields in space (each
  is raymarched or traced on its own) — except
  point figures (segment, vector, polyline, polygon, hull), which are cheap
  and allow 1024: a deformation drawn as
  arrows is `a = [0..20]; b = [0..20]; P = (a, b);
  f(x,y) = (x + y/2, y + sin(x)/2); vector(P, f(P))`. Shader members share
  one program with per-draw uniforms. Scalar fields/RGB fields/domain coloring/fractals cannot superimpose as
  families; use a selected list element. Point-list arithmetic works:
  `Q = P + (1,0)`, `2P`. `polyline(T)` / `polygon(T)` walk a whole tuple of
  points in order, `T = ((0, 0), (2, 0), (1, 1))`, and a list only once it
  is sorted: `polyline(sort(P, P.x))`, a CSV scatter
  `polyline(sort((data.x, data.y), data.x))`; a list `[ … ]` has no order to
  walk. `hull(P)` takes any list.
  Range bounds may use sliders, but not t; families re-expand on bound changes.
- Sequence values: `a_n = 1/n` defines `a_3` as a scalar and `a_[1..10]`
  as a list, usable in sums, scatters, histograms and regression. `a_k`
  reads the term at a slider `k`, and `a_N` one term per element of a list
  `N`. A term may use another sequence at its own index —
  `a_n = b_n + 1`, `b_[n+1] - b_n`, `sum(k=1..n, b_k)` — including a
  recurrence's terms (`d_n = a_{n+1} - a_n`, up to index 1000). A
  recurrence that steps from its own term alone draws a cobweb (or, with x,
  a bifurcation diagram). One whose step also reads n, another sequence at
  n, or a tuple at a position in n draws its terms as dots instead:
  `a_{n+1} = (n + 1) a_n` (factorials), `q_{n+1} = step(q_n, D[n + 1])`
  with `D = (1, 1, 0, 1)` (a state machine's run over the digits of D). Its
  terms stop where the tuple does. Two recurrences may read each other at n
  (`q_{n+1} = q_n + r_n` beside `r_{n+1} = r_n + q_n`), and a case in a
  sequence row may test equality (`{mod(n, 2) = 0: 1, 0}`). A sequence's
  index may also go in braces or parens, as its recurrence row is written: `b_{n+1}`, `a_(n-1)`,
  and the rows `a_{n} = 1/n` and `a_{0} = 1`. Each letter is one sequence: beside
  `a_n = 1/n`, `a_k = 7` is a constant named a_k. Indices
  must be whole numbers from 0 to 1000. Recurrences use their `a_0` seed
  (default 0.5); terms compute as a bounded chain of scalar constants, so
  sliders and t remain live. A recurrence using x as a bifurcation parameter
  cannot also supply constant terms without binding that parameter.
- Tuple-valued recurrences: a recurrence whose step calls `push(s, a)` (s
  with a appended) or `pop(s)` (s without its last element), or whose value
  is a tuple, has tuples as terms — a stack. `top(s)` reads the last
  element. `s_0 = ()` starts it from the empty tuple (the default), and any
  tuple may be its seed; a tuple seed with a step that makes no tuple
  (`a_0 = (0.1, 0.2); a_{n+1} = 3 a_n (1 - a_n)`) steps each element instead.
  `count(s_n)` is its length and `s_n[h]` its h-th element; a number with a
  tuple applies to each element (`1 + p_n`, `s_n/2`). Only the case that holds is run,
  so cases may differ in length: with `D = (1, 1, 2, 2)`,
  `s_{n+1} = {D[n + 1] = 1: push(s_n, 1), pop(s_n)}`. The run stops where
  it pops or reads the top of the empty tuple, or where no case holds (a
  machine with no move). The row draws its terms as rows of a lattice: row
  n, position h. A pushdown automaton is a state recurrence and a stack
  recurrence reading each other: `q_{n+1} = step(q_n, D[n + 1], top(s_n))`.
  One that starts from a point (`p_0 = (0, 0)`,
  `p_{n+1} = (1 - 1.4 p_n[1]^2 + p_n[2], 0.3 p_n[1])`, the Hénon map) and
  stays one draws its orbit as points. Other rows read its terms at a number
  or a slider (`s_3`, `top(s_k)`); an explicit sequence `d_n = count(s_n)`
  cannot (read it in a recurrence's step instead). Its terms are computed
  once, so its step cannot read t.
- Cellular automaton (1D): `c_{n+1}[i] = …` is a rule for a row of cells,
  reading the previous row at fixed offsets — `c_n[i-1]`, `c_n[i]`,
  `c_n[i+2]` — plus n, t and constants (not i itself). `c_0[i] = …` is the
  starting row as any expression in i; without it the start is a single 1
  at i = 0 on a background of 0s. The rule row draws the space-time diagram
  in a lattice panel (below): i across, n down, for 1000 steps. The lattice
  is unbounded: each side's background steps by the rule too, so rule 1
  (000 → 1) flips the whole background every row. Values shade the row's
  colour from 0 (empty) to the largest value (solid), so k-state rules work
  too. Every elementary rule on one slider:
  `r = 30; c_{n+1}[i] = mod(floor(r / 2^(4 c_n[i-1] + 2 c_n[i] + c_n[i+1])), 2)`
  (frame it with `view(i = -60..60, n = 0..80)`). In automaton and table rows
  a piecewise case may test equality — `{s = 3: 1, 0}` — since cells are
  whole numbers; so may a function those rows call.
- Cellular automaton (2D): `L_{n+1}[i, j] = …` reads the previous generation
  at fixed offsets, row first as in a matrix (`L_n[i+1, j]` is the cell
  below). A Σ with number bounds unrolls, so a neighbourhood is written once.
  The seed is `L_0[i, j] = …`, or the live cells as (row, column) points,
  `L_0 = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0), (2, 1), (2, 2)]` (a glider). The rule row
  draws one generation, 8 per second as t runs, on a board of cells
  -256..256 each way (a pattern reaching its edge is cut off there), with
  the generation read out in the corner. Conway's Life:
  `life(c, s) = {s = 3: 1, s = 4: c, 0}` then
  `L_{n+1}[i, j] = life(L_n[i, j], sum(a=-1..1, sum(b=-1..1, L_n[i+a, j+b])))`
  (s counts the cell itself).
- Table: `T[i, j] = …` is a function on the integer lattice, drawn as cells
  shaded by value: row i, column j, as a Cayley table or a matrix is read.
  Undefined values leave a cell empty, so nested cases bound it:
  `n = 6; T[i, j] = {0 <= i < n: {0 <= j < n: mod(i + j, n)}}` is the
  addition table of ℤ/n. Only the cells in view are computed, so a table
  may be unbounded (`T[i, j] = gcd(i, j)`).
- Graph: `graph(from, to)` or `graph(from, to, label)` draws arrows between
  numbered vertices, laid out automatically. Its arguments are read as one
  tuple whose elements are the arrows, so lists combine by the usual rule:
  with `k = [0..11]; g = [1, 4]`, `graph(k, mod(k + g, 12), g)` is the Cayley
  graph of ℤ/12 by 1 and 4 (both k's chosen together, g crossing them), and
  with `Q = [0..2]; S = [0, 1]` and a transition function `step(q, s)`,
  `graph(Q, step(Q, S), S)` is every transition of a state machine.
  `graph(P)` takes a list of pairs, `graph([(1, 2), (2, 3)])`. An arrow
  listed twice is drawn once with its count (×2); an undefined vertex drops
  its arrow, so a case keeps the ones wanted — composing two multisets of
  arrows (matrix multiplication, as paths): `graph({A.y = B.x: A.x}, B.y)`,
  or with the composition named as above, `graph(c(A, B))`.
  Cases in graph rows may test equality. A panel of graphs has no grid.
  A piecewise works inline over a list or through a function alike:
  `k = [1..40]; graph(k, {mod(k, 2) = 0: k/2, 3k + 1})`.
- `mark(v)` highlights vertex v in the graphs of its panel and reads v out;
  with a slider or t it walks, e.g. a state machine's run as a recurrence
  over a tuple of input symbols: `D = (1, 1, 0, 1); q_0 = 0;
  q_{n+1} = step(q_n, D[n + 1]); mark(q_N)`.
- Lattice panels: a panel whose rows are all automata, tables and stacks (or whose
  view row names index axes) is a lattice. Its grid runs between cells, its
  edges are numbered by index (whole numbers only), and zoomed in far enough
  each cell prints its value. `view(i = -60..60, n = 0..80)` frames one by
  its index names, in either order; panning rewrites it in those names.
- Decided comparisons: `2+2=4` reads “Always true (4 = 4)”; `e=2` reads
  “Never true (2.71828 ≠ 2)”. Comparisons involving sliders/time say
  “True now” or “False now”. They draw no degenerate implicit curve.
- Identities: an equation in x, y, z and t whose two sides agree everywhere
  reads “Holds everywhere (checked numerically)” instead of drawing a curve.
  The check compares both sides at many random points, for any slider
  values, so it is evidence, not a proof. `sin(x)^2 + cos(x)^2 = 1` holds;
  `sin(x)^2 + cos(x)^2 = 1.0001` does not, and stays an (empty) implicit
  curve. The wave equation for d'Alembert's solution:
  `c = 1; g(s) = exp(-s^2); f(x, t) = (g(x - c t) + g(x + c t))/2;
  y = f(x, t); d^2/dt^2 f(x, t) = c^2 ∇^2 f(x, t)`. The pulse splits in two
  and the last row holds everywhere. (u and w are the parametric and
  complex variables, so they cannot name the solution.)
- Vector field: a 2-tuple in x, y — `(-y, x)` — drawn as animated streamlines
  (line-integral convolution); clicking the canvas traces integral curves.
